title: Relational model, keys, constraints, ER modelling
scopeHtml: Scope: tables and SQL model, surrogate vs natural keys, foreign keys, constraints, NULL logic, ER modelling and common schema smells.

notes.title: What a relational database is
notes.html:
A relational database stores facts in tables (rows and columns) and lets you combine tables by matching values. A table is a set of rows; every row has the same columns; each column has a type. The "relational" word comes from math (a relation is a set of tuples), not from "relationships between tables".

The big idea: you describe WHAT you want (SQL), and the database figures out HOW to get it (the planner, covered in file 05). That is why the same query can stay correct while the engine gets faster.

Worked example. A users table with 10M rows, each row about 120 bytes: 10M x 120 B = 1.2 GB of heap, plus indexes. Postgres stores it in 8 KB pages, about 60 to 65 rows per page after the row header (23 bytes) and alignment, so roughly 160,000 pages.

CREATE TABLE users (
  id         bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  email      text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('a@x.com'), ('b@x.com');
SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE email = 'a@x.com';

Industry examples. Postgres runs Instagram's core data (they famously sharded it), Notion and Stripe-class payment ledgers. MySQL (InnoDB) powers Facebook's TAO storage tier and Uber's Schemaless-on-MySQL. SQLite is the same model embedded in every Android phone, which you already use through Room.

Postgres vs MySQL. Both speak SQL. Postgres has richer types (arrays, jsonb, ranges), partial indexes and RETURNING. MySQL InnoDB stores rows inside the primary-key B+tree (clustered); Postgres stores rows in an unordered heap and all indexes point to it. This one difference explains many later behaviours.

Everyday analogy. A set of spreadsheets where each sheet has a strict header, and you can ask "show me every order together with the customer's name" without the spreadsheets knowing about each other in advance.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "relational means tables are related". It is the math term for a set of tuples.
  • Thinking SQL says how to run the query. It is declarative; the planner chooses.
  • Forgetting a table has no guaranteed row order without ORDER BY.

notes.title: Keys: candidate, primary, alternate, surrogate
notes.html:
A key is a column (or set of columns) whose value identifies exactly one row. A candidate key is any minimal set of columns that is unique. You pick one as the primary key (PK); the others are alternate keys (enforce with UNIQUE).

Natural key = a real-world value (email, passport number, ISBN). Surrogate key = an invented value with no meaning (bigint identity, UUID). Surrogates win in practice because real-world values change (people change emails), are sometimes reused, and are often long.

Surrogate type Size Good Bad
bigint identity 8 B Small, ordered, index-friendly Guessable, hard to generate across shards
UUID v4 (random) 16 B Generate anywhere, unguessable Random inserts scatter across the B+tree, causing page splits and cache misses
UUID v7 / ULID (time-ordered) 16 B Generate anywhere AND ordered Leaks creation time; v7 needs a recent Postgres/library 
-- Natural key kept as an alternate key, surrogate as PK
CREATE TABLE country (
  id   smallint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  iso2 char(2) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name text NOT NULL
);

Worked example. Insert 100M rows with random UUID v4 PKs in InnoDB (clustered): each insert lands on a random leaf page, so after the working set exceeds the buffer pool (say 16 GB), almost every insert is a disk read plus later a page split. Teams report big throughput drops versus an auto-increment key. In Postgres the heap is append-friendly but the PK index still suffers the same random-leaf problem.

Industry examples. Stripe-style prefixed IDs (cus_...) are surrogates with a type tag. Twitter Snowflake IDs are 64-bit, time-ordered and generated on many machines, solving the "ordered but distributed" problem. Instagram's sharded Postgres built its own 64-bit time+shard+sequence IDs.

Decision gravity. Choosing the PK type is close to a one-way door: it is copied into every foreign key and every child index. Changing int to bigint later means rewriting huge tables. Default to bigint (an int overflows at 2.1 billion; teams have been woken at 3 a.m. by that) unless you have a reason.

Everyday analogy. Your name is a natural key (can change, can duplicate). Your student roll number is a surrogate: meaningless but stable and unique.

Common interview traps.

  • Using int PK on a table that can pass 2.1 billion rows.
  • Using email as PK and then needing to change an email across 20 child tables.
  • Saying UUIDs are "always slower"; random v4 is the issue, ordered ones are fine.

notes.title: Foreign keys and referential integrity
notes.html:
A foreign key (FK) says: this column's value must exist as a key in another table (or be NULL). It stops orphans: an order pointing to a customer who does not exist.

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  total_cents bigint NOT NULL CHECK (total_cents >= 0)
);
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_idx ON orders(customer_id);  -- Postgres does NOT do this for you

ON DELETE actions. RESTRICT/NO ACTION (refuse), CASCADE (delete children too), SET NULL, SET DEFAULT. Cascade is convenient and dangerous: deleting one tenant row can silently delete millions of rows and lock for minutes.

Key detail. Postgres does not auto-create an index on the referencing (child) column. Without it, deleting a parent row scans the whole child table to check for references, and joins are slow. MySQL InnoDB does create one automatically.

Worked example. orders has 50M rows, no index on customer_id. DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 7 runs a sequential scan of orders (about 6 GB read, seconds) while holding locks. With the index it is a sub-millisecond lookup.

Industry examples. Large-scale shops often drop FKs on the hottest tables (Shopify and GitHub have discussed online-schema-change and sharding reasons) and enforce integrity in application code plus periodic audit queries. The trade: speed and easy sharding versus lost guarantees.

Decision gravity. Adding an FK later to a big table is expensive but possible in Postgres: ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (takes a weaker lock). Removing one is easy. So start with FKs; drop them deliberately when measured.

Everyday analogy. A library loan card that must refer to a real member. The FK is the librarian refusing to log a loan for a made-up person.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting to index the FK column in Postgres.
  • Using ON DELETE CASCADE on a multi-tenant root table.
  • Claiming FKs are "too slow"; the cost is usually one index lookup per write, and the cost of orphan data is higher.

notes.title: Constraints: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, EXCLUDE
notes.html:
Constraints are rules the database enforces on every write, no matter which app or script writes. They are your last line of defence against bugs; app-level validation can be bypassed by a second service or a manual fix.

Constraint Meaning
NOT NULL Value required
UNIQUE No duplicates (implemented with a unique index). NULLs are allowed multiple times in Postgres (NULLs are not equal); Postgres 15 added UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT
CHECK Any boolean expression on the row
PRIMARY KEY UNIQUE + NOT NULL
EXCLUDE (Postgres) No two rows may "overlap", for example two bookings for the same room and time range 
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;
CREATE TABLE booking (
  room   int,
  during tstzrange,
  EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, during WITH &&)
);
INSERT INTO booking VALUES (1, '[2026-01-01 10:00, 2026-01-01 11:00)');
INSERT INTO booking VALUES (1, '[2026-01-01 10:30, 2026-01-01 11:30)');
-- ERROR: conflicting key value violates exclusion constraint

Worked example (race condition fixed by a constraint). App code does "SELECT if email exists, else INSERT". Two requests 5 ms apart both see "not exists" and both insert: two accounts, same email. A UNIQUE (email) makes the second insert fail with SQLSTATE 23505, which the app turns into "email taken". Correctness comes from the constraint, not the check.

Industry examples. Payment systems use UNIQUE (idempotency_key) so a retried request cannot charge twice (Stripe documents idempotency keys for this reason). Booking systems use exclusion constraints or unique (resource, slot) rows.

MySQL differences. MySQL enforces CHECK only from 8.0.16; before that it parsed and ignored it. No EXCLUDE. A unique index allows multiple NULLs too.

Decision gravity. Constraints are cheap to add early and painful to add to dirty data later (you must clean violations first). Treat them as reversible only before data is dirty.

Everyday analogy. The bouncer at the door versus a polite sign saying "please be 18". The sign is app validation; the bouncer is the constraint.

Common interview traps.

  • Check-then-insert in application code without a unique constraint.
  • Assuming UNIQUE blocks duplicate NULLs.
  • Storing money in float; use integer cents or numeric.

notes.title: Nulls and three-valued logic
notes.html:
NULL means "unknown", not zero and not empty string. Comparisons with NULL give UNKNOWN (neither true nor false). A WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is TRUE.

SELECT NULL = NULL;            -- NULL (unknown), not true
SELECT NULL IS NULL;           -- true
SELECT 5 NOT IN (1, 2, NULL);  -- NULL, so the row is dropped!
SELECT COALESCE(phone, 'n/a') FROM users;

The famous trap. x NOT IN (subquery) returns nothing if the subquery yields even one NULL. Use NOT EXISTS instead. Aggregates ignore NULLs (COUNT(col) skips them, COUNT(*) does not); AVG over {10, NULL, 20} is 15, not 10.

Worked example. orders has 1,000 rows, 100 with coupon IS NULL. WHERE coupon <> 'SAVE10' returns only rows with a non-null coupon different from SAVE10, so those 100 are missing. Fix: WHERE coupon IS DISTINCT FROM 'SAVE10'.

Design view. Many NULLs in a column often hint that the column belongs in a separate table (an optional 1:1 child). Oracle treats empty string as NULL; Postgres and MySQL do not.

Everyday analogy. A form field left blank: "I don't know your age" is different from "your age is 0".

Common interview traps.

  • WHERE col = NULL (never matches). Use IS NULL.
  • NOT IN with a nullable subquery.
  • Forgetting COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) difference.

notes.title: Entity-relationship modelling
notes.html:
ER modelling is drawing the nouns (entities), their facts (attributes) and how they connect (relationships) before creating tables. Interviews love it because it shows you can turn vague requirements into a schema.

Steps: (1) list nouns: User, Order, Product. (2) decide each one's identity (PK). (3) decide cardinality of every relationship. (4) turn into tables.

Relationship Example Table design
1:1 user and profile FK with UNIQUE on child, or same PK
1:N customer and orders FK on the "many" side
M:N students and courses Junction table with two FKs and a composite PK 
CREATE TABLE order_item (
  order_id   bigint REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  product_id bigint REFERENCES product(id),
  qty        int NOT NULL CHECK (qty > 0),
  unit_price_cents bigint NOT NULL,    -- snapshot, not a live lookup
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);

Key design lessons. (a) Snapshot prices in order_item; the product's price changes later but the old order must not. (b) The junction table is itself an entity and often grows its own columns (qty, enrolled_at). (c) Model "state" with a status column plus a history table when audits matter. (d) Soft delete (deleted_at) breaks UNIQUE unless you use a partial unique index: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users(email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL.

Worked example. Ride-hailing sketch: rider, driver, trip(rider_id, driver_id, status, fare_cents), location_ping(driver_id, ts, lat, lon). Pings are 1 per 4 s per driver; for 500k active drivers that is 125k writes/s, far too hot for the main relational DB, so pings go to a time-series or log store while trip stays relational. Knowing what NOT to put in the relational core is a senior signal.

Industry examples. Uber's trips and Airbnb's bookings are relational cores; the high-volume streams live elsewhere. Shopify's famous orders/line_items model is exactly the junction pattern above.

Decision gravity. Cardinality mistakes are one-way-ish: turning 1:N into M:N later means a new table and a backfill with downtime planning. Ask "can one X ever have many Y?" for every line.

Everyday analogy. Planning a school: students, teachers, classes. A class has many students and a student many classes, so you need an enrolment register in the middle.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting product_name and price live-joined into historical orders.
  • Modelling M:N with a comma-separated column.
  • Forgetting to ask whether a relationship can change over time (a customer's address history).

notes.title: Beyond the basics: keys at scale and common smells
notes.html:
Composite keys vs surrogate. A junction table naturally uses a composite PK (order_id, product_id). Column order matters for index use (file 04). Many ORMs prefer a single surrogate column; both are fine.

Smells to name in interviews.

  • EAV (entity-attribute-value): one table of (entity, attr, value). Flexible, but no types, no constraints, painful joins. Prefer jsonb for the truly dynamic part.
  • Polymorphic FK: (owner_type, owner_id) can't have a real FK. Prefer one FK column per target, or separate tables.
  • Storing lists in a column: violates 1NF (file 02).
  • Enum as string everywhere: use a lookup table or Postgres enum / CHECK; enum values are hard to remove in Postgres.
-- jsonb for genuinely sparse attributes, relational for the rest
ALTER TABLE product ADD COLUMN attrs jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}';
CREATE INDEX product_attrs_gin ON product USING gin (attrs);
SELECT id FROM product WHERE attrs @> '{"color":"red"}';

Industry examples. Shopify and GitLab use jsonb/JSON columns for flexible settings but keep money, status and relations in typed columns. Wikipedia's MediaWiki schema is a long-lived relational design on MySQL.

Decision gravity. jsonb is reversible in a weak way (you can extract to columns later) but queries and constraints on it are weaker; use it for attributes you will not join or constrain on.

Everyday analogy. A form with fixed boxes (typed columns) plus one "notes" box (jsonb). Notes are flexible, but you can't make the bank check them.

Common interview traps.

  • Recommending EAV because "schema is flexible".
  • Polymorphic associations with no integrity.
  • Using jsonb for everything and losing constraints and statistics.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• A relational DB stores sets of typed rows; SQL is declarative, the planner chooses the plan.
  • Prefer a bigint (or time-ordered UUID) surrogate PK; keep natural keys as UNIQUE. PK type is a near one-way door.
  • Foreign keys prevent orphans; in Postgres index the child column yourself; avoid CASCADE on big roots.
  • Constraints (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, EXCLUDE) are the real correctness layer; they fix check-then-insert races.
  • NULL is unknown: use IS NULL, IS DISTINCT FROM, NOT EXISTS instead of NOT IN.
  • ER modelling: nouns, identity, cardinality; M:N needs a junction table; snapshot historical values.
  • Avoid EAV and polymorphic FKs; use jsonb only for sparse, unconstrained attributes.

questions.promptHtml: What does "relational" actually mean in a relational database, and how does Postgres store a table differently from MySQL InnoDB?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who memorised "tables with foreign keys" from people who know the model and the storage engine consequences.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Relational comes from the math term relation: a set of tuples with the same typed columns. It is not about relationships between tables. You declare what you want in SQL and the planner decides how. Physically, Postgres keeps rows in an unordered heap and every index points to a row location, while InnoDB stores the row inside the primary-key B+tree, so the table is the primary index."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A relation is a set: no row order, no duplicate rows (SQL relaxes this to bags unless you have a key). Because the language is declarative, the same query can get faster when the engine gets a better plan, with no app change.

Storage consequence:

Postgres: heap pages (8 KB, unordered)   index leaf -> (page, slot) = ctid
InnoDB  : PK B+tree leaf = the full row  secondary index leaf -> PK value
  • Postgres: an UPDATE writes a new row version (MVCC) and may need new index entries unless HOT applies. A lookup by any index is one extra heap fetch.
  • InnoDB: lookup by secondary index finds the PK, then walks the PK tree again (double lookup). Random PKs fragment the clustered tree.
  • 10M rows at 120 B is about 1.2 GB heap in Postgres, roughly 60 rows per 8 KB page; verify the exact density with pg_relation_size.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('users')) AS heap,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_indexes_size('users'))  AS indexes;

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying relational means "tables are related by foreign keys".
  • Assuming row order without ORDER BY (heap order changes after UPDATE/VACUUM).
  • Treating MySQL and Postgres PK choice as equivalent.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does a wide PK hurt InnoDB more? -> Every secondary index leaf stores the PK, so a 16-byte UUID is copied into every index.
  2. Does a SELECT without ORDER BY return insertion order? -> Not guaranteed; it often looks that way until updates or parallel scans.
  3. What is ctid and why not use it as an ID? -> Physical location; changes on UPDATE and VACUUM FULL.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer describes tables and joins. The senior links the clustered vs heap layout to PK choice, index size and write amplification.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team moved to random UUID PKs on InnoDB and saw insert throughput fall as the working set outgrew the buffer pool.

questions.promptHtml: Explain candidate key, primary key, alternate key and superkey. Can a table have several, and can a primary key be NULL?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Basic vocabulary that the rest of normalization and indexing depends on.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A superkey is any column set that uniquely identifies a row. A candidate key is a minimal superkey: remove any column and uniqueness breaks. The primary key is the candidate I pick as the main identifier; the others are alternate keys, enforced with UNIQUE NOT NULL. A table has one PK, many candidate keys, and PK columns can never be NULL."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Example employee(id, email, passport_no, dept, name):

  • Superkeys: {id}, {id, name}, {email, dept}...
  • Candidate keys: {id}, {email}, {passport_no} (minimal).
  • PK: id. Alternate keys: email, passport_no.

The PK implies NOT NULL + UNIQUE and gets a unique index. A composite key such as order_items(order_id, product_id) is minimal only as a pair. UNIQUE columns allow NULLs in Postgres (multiple NULLs are distinct), so an alternate key must also be NOT NULL to be a true key.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
CREATE TABLE employee (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  email text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  passport_no text UNIQUE            -- nullable: not a full key for rows without one
);

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling any unique column a candidate key without checking NULLs.
  • Thinking a composite key must be built from a surrogate plus something.
  • Believing there can be only one UNIQUE constraint.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is {id, name} a candidate key? -> No, it is a superkey; name is redundant.
  2. Can a PK be changed? -> Yes, but FKs referencing it need ON UPDATE CASCADE; best treated as immutable.
  3. Why does a composite PK matter for column order? -> The B-tree index supports prefix lookups, so (a,b) serves a but not b alone.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer lists definitions. The senior adds the NULL caveat for UNIQUE and that keys are business rules the schema must enforce, not just an index.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "unique" email column without NOT NULL let a bulk import create 40k rows with NULL emails that broke login-by-email.

questions.promptHtml: What is three-valued logic in SQL, and why does WHERE col <> 5 not return rows where col is NULL?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: NULL bugs silently return wrong data. This is the most common source of wrong reports.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "NULL means unknown, so comparisons with it yield UNKNOWN, not true or false. WHERE keeps only rows where the predicate is TRUE, so UNKNOWN rows are dropped. col <> 5 with col NULL is UNKNOWN, and the row disappears. To include them I use IS DISTINCT FROM or an explicit OR col IS NULL."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Truth tables: TRUE AND UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN, FALSE AND UNKNOWN = FALSE, TRUE OR UNKNOWN = TRUE, NOT UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN.

  • NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN, not true. Use IS NULL.
  • CHECK constraints pass on UNKNOWN (only FALSE rejects), WHERE fails on UNKNOWN. This asymmetry bites.
  • Aggregates skip NULLs: avg(x) divides by the non-null count; count(*) counts rows, count(x) non-null.
  • GROUP BY and DISTINCT treat NULLs as equal (one group), unlike =.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
SELECT 1 WHERE NULL = NULL;                 -- no row
SELECT 1 WHERE NULL IS NOT DISTINCT FROM NULL;  -- row
SELECT count(*), count(discount), avg(discount) FROM orders;

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• WHERE x = NULL (never true).
  • NOT IN (subquery) where the subquery yields a NULL returns zero rows.
  • Assuming CHECK (age > 0) blocks NULL.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you sort NULLs? -> Postgres puts them last in ASC by default; use NULLS FIRST/LAST.
  2. Does UNIQUE treat NULLs as equal? -> No in Postgres (multiple allowed); Postgres 15 adds NULLS NOT DISTINCT.
  3. How do you do a null-safe join? -> ON a.x IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.x, which usually cannot use a plain index efficiently; consider a sentinel or coalesce index.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "NULL is not equal to anything". The senior states the WHERE/CHECK asymmetry and lists the places NULL is treated as equal (GROUP BY, DISTINCT, UNION).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A churn report filtering plan <> 'free' silently excluded every user with NULL plan, understating churn by 12%.

questions.contextHtml:
A coupon system. Product asks: "show orders that did not use the SUMMER10 coupon" and "make sure a user has at most one active coupon".

CREATE TABLE orders (id bigint PRIMARY KEY, user_id bigint, coupon text, total int);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_active ON user_coupons (user_id, redeemed_at);

SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE coupon <> 'SUMMER10';          -- returns 6,100
SELECT count(*) FROM orders;                                     -- returns 10,000
SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE coupon IS NULL;                -- returns 3,400

Active coupons have redeemed_at IS NULL. Support complains some users have 3 active coupons. The first count looks low compared to expectations (finance expects 7,000+).
questions.promptHtml: Find both bugs, explain them, and fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more data checks" or only spots one bug. Does not notice that unique indexes allow many NULLs, or reaches for COALESCE everywhere without thinking about index use.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does NULL coupon mean "no coupon used"? (yes, 3,400). Is "active" defined as redeemed_at NULL? Postgres version (for NULLS NOT DISTINCT)? Are duplicates already in prod?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the report query; for duplicates, stop the bleeding by marking extras inactive in a one-off job.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) <> drops NULL rows: 10,000 - 3,400 NULL - 500 SUMMER10 = 6,100, matches exactly. (b) The unique index treats each NULL redeemed_at as distinct. Red herring: replication lag or a race, the arithmetic already explains the count.
  4. How I'd verify each: SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE coupon='SUMMER10') to confirm 500; SELECT user_id, count(*) FROM user_coupons WHERE redeemed_at IS NULL GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*)>1.
  5. Root cause: Three-valued logic: UNKNOWN rows are filtered out by WHERE, and unique indexes consider NULLs distinct so (user, NULL) can repeat.
  6. Fix: Short term WHERE coupon IS DISTINCT FROM 'SUMMER10'. Long term a partial unique index:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_active ON user_coupons (user_id) WHERE redeemed_at IS NULL;
  1. Prevention: Review checklist item: "every predicate on a nullable column: what about NULL?" Add a test with a NULL row in fixtures.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not use sentinel dates like 1970-01-01 to avoid NULL; it pollutes range logic. The partial index is smaller too.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if MySQL? -> MySQL has no partial indexes, so a stored generated column active_user = IF(redeemed_at IS NULL, user_id, NULL) with a UNIQUE index works (NULLs stay distinct for the non-active rows), or use a separate active_coupon table keyed by user_id.
  • Existing duplicates block index creation? -> Dedupe first, then CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fraud report undercounted flagged accounts for months because flag <> 'none' skipped NULL flags written by an older service. The fix was a NOT NULL DEFAULT backfill.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Finds neither bug or blames data quality.
  • Hire: Explains <> dropping NULLs and proposes IS DISTINCT FROM.
  • Strong hire: Also spots the unique-NULL issue, uses a partial unique index, and plans safe backfill and concurrent index build.

questions.promptHtml: Surrogate key or natural key as primary key? When would you pick each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests judgment, not trivia. Wrong choices are expensive to undo.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Default to a surrogate key (bigint identity) as PK because it is small, stable and meaningless, so nothing outside needs to change when business data changes. I still declare the natural key as UNIQUE NOT NULL so the business rule is enforced. I use a natural key only when it is truly immutable and small, like ISO country code, or for join tables where the pair is the identity."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Natural keys change: emails change, phone numbers get reassigned, even government IDs get corrected. A PK change cascades through every FK and every index that stores the key. Costs and benefits:

Surrogate: 8 B, monotonic, FKs and secondary indexes stay small, exposes nothing
Natural  : no extra join/lookup to fetch meaning, self-documenting, but may be wide and mutable

Trap: using only a surrogate and forgetting the UNIQUE on the natural key lets duplicates in ("two Ashas with the same email"). Exposing sequential ids in URLs leaks volume and enables enumeration; use a separate public id or opaque token for that.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
CREATE TABLE country (code char(2) PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL);  -- ISO, immutable
CREATE TABLE users (
  id    bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  email text NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT users_email_uq UNIQUE (email)
);

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Surrogate PK with no UNIQUE on the real identity.
  • Using email as PK "because it is unique".
  • Exposing the surrogate id as a security boundary.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Composite natural key on a join table? -> Fine and usually best: (order_id, product_id).
  2. Case-insensitive email uniqueness? -> citext or a unique index on lower(email).
  3. Does surrogate help partitioning? -> Not by itself; partition keys are chosen by access pattern.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "surrogate is faster". The senior says "mutability and width drive it, and always keep the natural UNIQUE".

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A company used SSN-like national IDs as PK; a regulatory change forced re-keying 30 tables.

questions.contextHtml:
Postgres 15, customers 2M rows, orders 80M rows with customer_id REFERENCES customers(id). Nightly cleanup runs DELETE FROM customers WHERE id IN (...) for 5,000 inactive customers. It used to take 3 seconds; last night it ran 40 minutes, holding locks, and the API timed out on signups. orders.customer_id has no index (someone dropped it to save disk). pg_stat_activity shows one backend running the delete; auto_explain-style output:

-- illustrative
Trigger for constraint orders_customer_id_fkey: time=2410000.1 calls=5000

CPU is moderate, disk reads high. A red herring: replication lag is also up.
questions.promptHtml: Why is the delete so slow and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more CPU" or "batch it" without finding the cause. Doesn't know FK checks are triggers that scan the child table.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the FK action (NO ACTION/CASCADE)? Was an index dropped recently? Are the deleted customers expected to have orders?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cancel the job (pg_cancel_backend), it only held the delete's locks; re-run later in small batches after the index exists.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Missing index on child FK column: each deleted parent triggers a seq scan of 80M rows. (b) Cascading delete volume. (c) Lock waits. The trigger timing line points to (a).
  4. How I'd verify each: \d orders for indexes; SELECT * FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname='orders' shows seq_scan climbing; test one delete with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) on a replica.
  5. Root cause: Postgres does not auto-index the referencing column. On parent delete it runs SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1 FOR KEY SHARE, which seq-scans 80M rows 5,000 times. Scale: 5,000 x ~8 s per scan is about 11 hours worst case; caching made it 40 min.
  6. Fix: Short term CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_customer_id_idx ON orders(customer_id); then delete in batches of 500. Long term keep the index as part of the migration standard.
  7. Prevention: A CI query listing FKs without a supporting index (compare pg_constraint with pg_index).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not drop the FK to "speed things up"; integrity bugs cost more than 40 MB of index. Not run with session_replication_role=replica.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would MySQL behave the same? -> InnoDB requires an index on FK columns and creates one automatically.
  • What about ON DELETE CASCADE? -> Same lookup plus the child deletes; index is even more critical.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A cleanup of 1% of rows locked a hot parent table for 25 minutes. The cure was one index and batching in 1,000-row transactions.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests hardware or kill and retry.
  • Hire: Identifies missing FK index and builds it concurrently.
  • Strong hire: Explains the trigger mechanism, batches, and adds a CI check for unindexed FKs.

questions.promptHtml: Compare ON DELETE CASCADE, SET NULL, RESTRICT and NO ACTION. Which would you use for orders to customers and why?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Cascades can silently delete large amounts of data. Tests risk awareness.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "RESTRICT and NO ACTION reject deleting a parent with children; the difference is when the check runs (RESTRICT immediately, NO ACTION at statement end and deferrable). CASCADE deletes children. SET NULL orphans them explicitly. For orders referencing customers I use RESTRICT: financial records must not vanish, so a customer is anonymised or soft-deleted instead."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Parent delete -> FK trigger ->  RESTRICT/NO ACTION: error
                                CASCADE: delete child rows (recursive)
                                SET NULL / SET DEFAULT: update child column
  • CASCADE is right for true ownership: order_items belong to orders. It is dangerous across domains: deleting a customer cascades into orders, payments, invoices.
  • Cascades are row-by-row inside one transaction; a parent with 5M children means a huge transaction, WAL burst and long locks.
  • SET NULL requires the child column nullable, which weakens the model.
  • Deferrable constraints (DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED) allow temporarily inconsistent state inside a transaction, useful for circular inserts.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id   bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  product_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Cascading from reference/master data to transactions.
  • Forgetting an index on the child FK column.
  • Assuming CASCADE fires triggers in the same order across tables.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to delete a customer for GDPR but keep orders? -> Anonymise PII, keep the row and key.
  2. Does CASCADE produce audit logs? -> Only if triggers/logical decoding capture each deleted row.
  3. Cyclic FKs? -> Use DEFERRABLE or insert then UPDATE.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer defines each option. The senior ties the choice to ownership boundaries and operational blast radius.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cascading delete of one test tenant wiped 14M rows across 9 tables and filled the WAL disk.

questions.contextHtml: A meeting-room booking service on Postgres. bookings(id, room_id, starts_at, ends_at). The app checks for overlap with a SELECT, then INSERTs. Under load (about 300 booking requests/sec at 9 AM) support finds double-booked rooms: 23 overlaps last week. Someone proposes a unique index on (room_id, starts_at). Another suggests locking the whole table. Logs show two requests inserting 10:00-11:00 and 10:30-11:30 within 4 ms.
questions.promptHtml: How do you make double booking impossible at the database level?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a unique index on room and start time" (does not catch partial overlap) or "use an app-level mutex" (breaks with multiple instances).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are ranges half-open? Can a booking be cancelled (soft state)? Single region primary? Postgres version?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add an advisory lock per room around the check+insert while I build the constraint; clean the 23 overlaps by hand.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Check-then-insert race (classic TOCTOU). The unique index on start time cannot express overlap. Table lock would work but serialises all rooms.
  4. How I'd verify each: Query self-join for overlaps; reproduce with two psql sessions at READ COMMITTED.
  5. Root cause: Under READ COMMITTED neither transaction sees the other's uncommitted row, both pass the check. Overlap is a range condition, not equality.
  6. Fix: An exclusion constraint:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;
ALTER TABLE bookings
  ADD COLUMN during tstzrange GENERATED ALWAYS AS (tstzrange(starts_at, ends_at, '[)')) STORED,
  ADD CONSTRAINT no_overlap EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&)
      WHERE (status = 'active');

The engine rejects the second insert with SQLSTATE 23P01; the app retries or shows "taken". 7. Prevention: Add a CHECK ends_at > starts_at; test with concurrent inserts in CI. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rely on SERIALIZABLE alone (works but needs retry logic and costs more); not lock the whole table. GiST index adds write cost, acceptable at 300/s.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• MySQL? -> No EXCLUDE; use a slot table (one row per room per 15 min with a UNIQUE key) or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a room row.
  • Cancelled bookings? -> The WHERE clause on the constraint ignores them.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A clinic scheduling system had 0.3% double bookings that "could not happen" because the app checked first. An exclusion constraint turned it into a clean 409 response.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: App-level check only.
  • Hire: Knows the race and proposes a DB-level mechanism.
  • Strong hire: Uses EXCLUDE with range types, partial predicate, and explains the retry and MySQL alternative.

questions.contextHtml: Interview prompt: "Design the schema for a course platform. Students enrol in courses, courses have instructors, and we want to track the grade and enrolment date." The interviewer stops there. Scale hint when asked: 2M students, 20k courses, 40M enrolments, a course can have co-instructors, a student can retake a course.
questions.promptHtml: Walk through your ER model and the DDL.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Puts course_ids as a comma list on student, or a student-course table with only two FKs and the grade on the student table. Misses retakes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can a student retake, and do we keep every attempt? Do grades change after publishing (history)? Are course offerings per term? Is an instructor per offering or per course?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design). I state assumptions out loud: retakes allowed, per-term offerings.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Alternatives: (a) student-course M:N; (b) student-offering M:N where offering = course + term. (b) wins because grade and instructors belong to the offering.
  4. How I'd verify each: Walk three queries: "transcript of student X", "class roster of offering Y", "average grade of course Z across terms".
  5. Root cause: An M:N relationship with its own attributes becomes an entity (enrolment). Its identity is (student, offering), and a retake is a new offering so the key still holds.
  6. Fix (DDL):
CREATE TABLE course   (id bigint PRIMARY KEY, code text NOT NULL UNIQUE, title text NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE offering (id bigint PRIMARY KEY, course_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES course,
                       term text NOT NULL, UNIQUE (course_id, term));
CREATE TABLE offering_instructor (offering_id bigint REFERENCES offering,
                       instructor_id bigint REFERENCES instructor, PRIMARY KEY (offering_id, instructor_id));
CREATE TABLE enrolment (student_id bigint REFERENCES student, offering_id bigint REFERENCES offering,
                       enrolled_on date NOT NULL, grade numeric(4,1) CHECK (grade BETWEEN 0 AND 100),
                       PRIMARY KEY (student_id, offering_id));
CREATE INDEX ON enrolment (offering_id);   -- roster lookups
  1. Prevention: Draw cardinalities, check every FK has an index serving a real query.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not store grade history inline; if audit is required, add enrolment_grade_history. Not use arrays for relationships.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Waitlists? -> Add a status column or separate table; add partial unique index for active enrolment.
  • Scale to 400M enrolments? -> Partition by term; PK includes it only if needed, or keep a global unique via offering_id since offering encodes term.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A platform modelled student-course directly; adding "retake" two years later forced a re-key of 30M rows.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Lists tables without cardinalities.
  • Hire: Models M:N with attributes as an entity and a composite PK.
  • Strong hire: Surfaces offering vs course, retakes, indexes for the access pattern, and states assumptions.

questions.promptHtml: UUID v4, bigint identity or UUID v7 as a primary key: how do they behave at hundreds of millions of rows in Postgres and InnoDB?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: PK choice is hard to change and affects write throughput, index size and security.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Random UUID v4 inserts land on random B-tree leaves, so the whole index must be cached, pages split, and WAL grows from full-page writes. Bigint identity is compact and append-only, but needs coordination across shards and leaks counts. UUID v7 is time-ordered, so it keeps insert locality like a sequence while still being generated anywhere. I default to bigint for single-primary OLTP and v7 when ids must be generated client-side or across shards."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
bigint / UUIDv7 : inserts hit the right-most leaf -> hot pages stay cached
UUIDv4          : inserts hit random leaves -> cache misses, page splits (~50-70% fill)

Sizes: bigint 8 B, uuid 16 B. On InnoDB the PK is copied into every secondary index, so a 16 B key across 5 indexes adds 80 B per row; at 500M rows that is about 40 GB more (rough, verify). On Postgres, indexes hold ctid, not the PK, so the damage is limited to the PK index and FK indexes, but random order still means full-page WAL writes after each checkpoint. v7 leaks creation time; that is usually fine but know it. Native uuidv7() arrived in Postgres 18 (verify); before that use an extension or app-side generator.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
-- Postgres 17 and older: app generates UUIDv7; column is plain uuid
CREATE TABLE events (id uuid PRIMARY KEY, payload jsonb NOT NULL);
-- illustrative sizes
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('events_pkey'));

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Storing UUIDs as varchar(36) (36+ bytes, slower compares).
  • Using v4 as clustered key on InnoDB without binary(16) packing.
  • Believing sequential ids are a security feature or flaw by themselves; authorisation is the control.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not snowflake ids? -> Fine (64-bit, ordered) but needs a worker-id scheme and clock-skew handling.
  2. Bigint overflow risk? -> int4 maxes at 2.1B; use bigint from day one.
  3. Public ids? -> Keep an internal bigint plus an opaque public token column.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "UUIDs are slower". The senior quantifies locality, page splits, index size per engine and names the generation constraint driving the choice.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A write-heavy service on random UUID PKs hit buffer-cache thrash at 300M rows; moving to time-ordered ids cut p99 insert latency by roughly 5x.

questions.contextHtml:
Postgres 14, payments has 600M rows (900 GB), 4,000 writes/sec. Orphan rows exist: about 12k payments reference deleted orders. You need payments.order_id NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id). A teammate ran this on staging (1 GB) in 200 ms:

ALTER TABLE payments ADD CONSTRAINT fk_order FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES orders(id);
ALTER TABLE payments ALTER COLUMN order_id SET NOT NULL;

Production SLO: no write stall over 2 seconds. Red herring: staging has no concurrent traffic.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Run it in a maintenance window", or runs it directly and the validation scan holds a lock for 20 minutes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can I tolerate orphans being fixed or archived? Postgres version for the NOT NULL trick? Is there a replica lag budget? Business owner for orphans?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed yet; first I'd stop anyone running the naive DDL.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: ADD FOREIGN KEY takes SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE and validates all 600M rows under that lock, blocking writes. SET NOT NULL does a full scan under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE.
  4. How I'd verify each: Test on a restored clone of similar size; watch pg_locks and pg_stat_progress_*.
  5. Root cause: Validation work happens while a strong lock is held, and the 12k orphans would fail it anyway.
  6. Fix: Expand in steps:
ALTER TABLE payments ADD CONSTRAINT fk_order FOREIGN KEY (order_id)
  REFERENCES orders(id) NOT VALID;               -- brief lock, new writes checked
-- resolve orphans in batches (archive or repoint), then:
ALTER TABLE payments VALIDATE CONSTRAINT fk_order;  -- SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, writes continue
ALTER TABLE payments ADD CONSTRAINT oid_nn CHECK (order_id IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE payments VALIDATE CONSTRAINT oid_nn;
ALTER TABLE payments ALTER COLUMN order_id SET NOT NULL;  -- PG12+ uses the valid CHECK, no rescan
ALTER TABLE payments DROP CONSTRAINT oid_nn;

Set lock_timeout = '3s' and retry so DDL never queues behind a long transaction and blocks everyone. 7. Prevention: Migration linter that bans non-NOT-VALID FK additions on large tables; a staging dataset with production-scale rows. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not delete orphans blindly (finance may need them); not disable triggers. Validation still scans 900 GB and adds IO; run it off-peak.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Validation takes 40 minutes: risk? -> Long snapshot holds back vacuum; acceptable but monitor bloat.
  • MySQL? -> Use online DDL / gh-ost; FK validation differs.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "quick" FK add blocked checkout for 11 minutes because a long report transaction made the ALTER wait and queued every writer behind it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Runs it as is or in a window.
  • Hire: Uses NOT VALID then VALIDATE.
  • Strong hire: Handles orphans, lock_timeout, the CHECK-then-SET NOT NULL trick and lock queueing.

questions.contextHtml:
events.id is serial (int4), 1.9 billion rows, growing 25M/day. Max is 2,147,483,647, so about 10 days of headroom (about 247M ids left). Table is 700 GB, 3 secondary indexes, referenced by 4 child tables with int4 FKs. Writes are 400/sec steady, no maintenance window. Alert sample:

ERROR:  nextval: reached maximum value of sequence "events_id_seq" (2147483647)  -- what you will see on day 10

A teammate suggests ALTER TABLE events ALTER COLUMN id TYPE bigint. Red herring: disk is 40% free.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Runs the ALTER TYPE, which rewrites 700 GB under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for hours.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do clients depend on the column type (ORMs, Kafka schemas)? Is the table partitioned? Are the 4 children also huge? Is downtime ever allowed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Buy time: ALTER SEQUENCE ... MINVALUE -2147483648 RESTART -2147483648-style tricks use the negative half (about 2.1B more ids) if ordering assumptions allow. That gives months.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: N/A for diagnosis; the options are (a) negative-range stopgap, (b) online bigint migration, (c) new partitioned table with bigint.
  4. How I'd verify each: Check SELECT last_value FROM events_id_seq, check dependants with \d+, test ordering assumptions (code that does ORDER BY id).
  5. Root cause: int4 chosen at design time for a table that grows without bound.
  6. Fix: Online migration: add id_new bigint, backfill in batches of 50k with a trigger copying new rows, build a unique index CONCURRENTLY, swap in a short transaction:
ALTER TABLE events ADD COLUMN id_new bigint;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY events_id_new_uq ON events(id_new);
-- backfill in batches, trigger sets id_new := id for new rows, then in one short txn:
-- swap names, move default to a bigint sequence, repoint PK USING INDEX

Repeat for the four child FK columns. Alternatively create a partitioned bigint table and attach. 7. Prevention: Lint rule: new PKs must be bigint; alert at 50% of sequence max. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rewrite in place; not delete old data as a fix if retention requires it. The migration takes weeks of low-priority IO but zero downtime.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Sequence hits max early during the migration? -> Use the negative stopgap first.
  • Clients parse id as 32-bit? -> Coordinate API versioning before cutover.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team learned about int4 overflow from a 3 AM page; the negative-range stopgap bought 11 weeks to finish the migration.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: In-place ALTER during peak.
  • Hire: Online add-column and backfill.
  • Strong hire: Stopgap sequence range, child FKs, client compatibility and monitoring.

questions.contextHtml:
A product team stores customer-defined fields in a table attributes(entity_id, key, value text) (EAV). 5M entities, 60 attributes each, so 300M rows. Reports like "customers in Pune with plan=pro and seats>10" need three self-joins and are timing out (EXPLAIN shows nested loops, 40 s, illustrative):

-- illustrative
Nested Loop  (actual time=0.9..40211 rows=812)
  -> Index Scan using attr_key_value on attributes a1 (rows=1.2M)
  -> Index Scan using attr_pkey on attributes a2 ... loops=1200000

Values are all text so seats > 10 is a string comparison and returns wrong rows ('9' > '10'). PM wants "flexible schema, no migrations".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more indexes". Or "EAV is always wrong" with no alternative for truly dynamic fields.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which attributes are fixed and queried vs truly tenant-defined? How many distinct keys? Are searches ad hoc or a known set? Read/write ratio?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cast and filter by typed expression for the bad comparison, add a materialised wide view for the top three reports.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Join fan-out from self-joins; type loss on text; no per-attribute statistics so the planner misestimates.
  4. How I'd verify each: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS); SELECT key, count(*) FROM attributes GROUP BY 1 to see which 10 keys carry 90% of queries.
  5. Root cause: EAV moves the schema into data, losing types, constraints, FKs and planner statistics.
  6. Fix: Hybrid model: promote the known hot attributes to real typed columns; keep the long tail in jsonb with a GIN index:
ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN city text, ADD COLUMN plan text, ADD COLUMN seats int;
ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN extra jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}';
CREATE INDEX ON customers (city, plan);
CREATE INDEX ON customers USING gin (extra jsonb_path_ops);
  1. Prevention: Policy: any attribute used in 3+ queries or any filter gets promoted; schema review for new "flexible" tables.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not make everything jsonb (stats are weak, constraints awkward). Not keep pure EAV. Keep typed CHECKs for promoted columns.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Tenant defines 500 custom fields? -> jsonb plus an attribute catalog for validation.
  • Migration without downtime? -> Dual write, backfill in batches, switch reads, drop EAV rows.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A CRM's EAV table reached 2B rows and every new report was a month of tuning; promoting 12 columns removed 90% of the query load.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: More indexes only.
  • Hire: Proposes typed columns for the hot set.
  • Strong hire: Hybrid with jsonb and GIN, discusses stats, constraints and migration.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident: users could not re-register after deleting their account ("email already exists"), and separately 300 ghost accounts shared one email because a bug path created rows with deleted_at set. The schema:

CREATE TABLE users (id bigint PRIMARY KEY, email text NOT NULL, deleted_at timestamptz,
                    CONSTRAINT users_email_key UNIQUE (email));

Soft-deleted rows stay for 90 days for legal reasons. In the incident someone "fixed" it by dropping the UNIQUE constraint; two live accounts then registered with Ann@x.com and ann@x.com.
questions.promptHtml: Run the review: causes, correct design, and how to roll it out.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Drop the constraint and check in code", which created the second incident.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should a deleted email be reusable immediately? Is email case-insensitive? Can several deleted rows share an email? Do other tables (sessions) point to deleted users?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Re-add uniqueness for live rows only, after merging the duplicate live accounts manually.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Constraint scope was too wide (all rows), then removed entirely; no case normalisation.
  4. How I'd verify each: SELECT lower(email), count(*) FROM users WHERE deleted_at IS NULL GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*)>1;
  5. Root cause: The business rule is "unique among live users, case-insensitive", but it was expressed as a plain unique on a raw column, then abandoned.
  6. Fix:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY users_live_email_uq
  ON users (lower(email)) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
ALTER TABLE users DROP CONSTRAINT users_email_key;   -- after the new index is valid

Queries must use lower(email) to hit the index; or use citext. 7. Prevention: Constraint reviews in the PR template ("what is the actual uniqueness scope?"); a test that registers, deletes, re-registers. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rely on application checks (races). Not hard-delete if legal retention applies. Partial indexes cannot back a foreign key, so FKs still point to id.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Unique on (email) where status='active' in MySQL? -> Generated column trick or separate table.
  • Dedupe of 300 ghosts first? -> Yes, index creation fails otherwise; use a ROW_NUMBER() pass to pick survivors.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "delete account" feature shipped with a global UNIQUE; the fix was a one-line partial index and a week of support tickets.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Drops constraints or relies on code.
  • Hire: Partial unique index on live rows.
  • Strong hire: Adds case-insensitivity, safe concurrent migration, FK limitations, and prevention in review.
